How to value any token from its cash flows (+ what you need): 👇 

> You need a spreadsheet
> 4 free sites
> A few hours
> Or use my free bot (link at the end)

Where do you get the data?
 > DefiLlama: fees, revenue, holder revenue > CoinGecko: price and supply > The protocol's docs: fee routing, allocation, vesting > The US 10-year yield and Damodaran's country risk table

Step 1: Find holder earnings (E0)
 • Download daily fees, revenue and holders revenue from DefiLlama • Whole days only. Skip today. • E0 = the last 365 days of holders revenue • Under a year: take the lower of the 90-day total and the 14-day total scaled to a year • Under 30 days of history: stop • Only count money that reaches holders • Tokens paid out as new issuance are dilution, not earnings • EPS = E0 ÷ total supply

Step 2: Work out supply
 • Use total outstanding supply, not circulating • Include vested tokens nobody has claimed • If tokens are unissued, check two things: do the team wallets hold the biggest balance, and do fees alone fund operations and buybacks? • Both true: count 60% of the unissued pool (base), 10% (bull), 0% (bear) • Otherwise: 100% (bear), 60% (base), 10% (bull) • Run both versions and compare

Step 3: Build the discount rate (Ke)
 • Add: risk-free rate + equity risk premium (about 4–6%) + regulatory + governance + alignment + smart-contract risk • Alignment: 0% automatic, 1% changeable, 2% decided case by case • Smart-contract risk: about 2% after a big exploit, about 0.5% if battle-tested • Under 90 days old: add up to 2 points • Long-run rate: same layers, smart-contract risk at its floor

Step 4: Choose 7 years of growth
 • Take the category's trailing fee growth from DefiLlama • Base = a third of that, capped at 20% a year • Bull = +10 points, bear = −10 points • Category down sharply from its peak? Start from the lower level • Structural decline: base growth 0%
Step 5: Estimate the exit multiple • Judge the moat and pick a return on equity (ROE): 20% for weak, 100%+ for strong • No moat: ROE = long-run Ke • Long-run growth (gT): 3.0% bear, 3.5% base, 4.5% bull • P/E = (1 − gT ÷ ROE) ÷ (long-run Ke − gT)

Step 6: Calculate value per token
 • Grow earnings each year: E(t) = E0 × (1 + g)^t • Divide by that year's supply: add vested or emitted tokens, subtract burned ones • Discount each year by (1 + Ke)^t and add up all 7 • Exit value = P/E × year-7 EPS, discounted back 7 years • Fair value = discounted payouts + discounted exit • Repeat for bear, base and bull, then weight 20/60/20

Step 7: Compare with price
 • Fair value vs today's price, as a % above or below • Break-even growth: change base growth until your value equals the price (goal-seek does this) • That's the growth the market is already pricing in

Step 8: Check yourself
 • Do the three scenarios look sensible together? • Does one changed assumption swing the answer? That input is carrying the result. • Write down every guess you couldn't verify • Rerun with the other emissions setting

Fees not reaching holders yet?
 • Value it twice: once as if nothing reaches holders, once with the fee switch on or buybacks restarted • Weight the second case by your own odds, e.g. 40% within a year if buybacks are only paused
Keep a record • Note every number's source and the date you got it • Label your own judgement calls as yours

Bookmark this and follow for the next build.

If we take the view that power becomes the ultimate bottleneck, the capex optimization constraint shifts to the one input China has in greater abundance vs US (who has relatively more chips)

Then if you take the view that global token spend increasingly flows to cheap power and open weights, spot market is likely where China’s marginal impact would show up first via token dumping, esp if the future of work is mostly inference based not training (which also requires excess capacity with lower utilization rates)

So the compute forward curve actually becomes an epic industrial duration battle where China competes at the front end and the US holds the long end. The question then becomes who is the dog and who is the tail, and which strategic advantage will roll down the curve faster- chips or power? I think anyone who understands the leverage of depreciation knows the answer.

In other words this is a warning to US policymakers: the long end of the compute curve was never really about contracted chips security. It’s about energized megawatts and that’s basically the one duration the US is shortest vs its biggest geopolitical rival
